tagline.text: A northern city welcoming you with a sinking bell tower and the scent of longganisa

items.credit: Ralff Nestor Nacor / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: The capital of Ilocos Norte and the gateway to travel in northwestern Luzon. Walk the brick bell tower that sinks a little deeper into the ground each year, along with a cathedral with 400 years of history, taste Laoag longganisa and empanada, then head on to the sand dunes, Paoay, and Pagudpud.
Laoag is the capital of Ilocos Norte, about
480km
north of Manila, a city of roughly 110,000 people set on the plain at the mouth of the Laoag River. Its name is said to mean "light" in Ilocano, and it became a city in

. With an international airport, a long-distance bus terminal, malls, and hotels all clustered together, it serves as the starting point for a swing through Ilocos Norte that continues on to Paoay Church, La Paz Sand Dunes, the Bangui windmills, and Pagudpud.
The city's history begins with its Spanish colonial-era church. The Augustinians built the first church of wood and thatch in
, and today's St. William's Cathedral, whose foundation was laid in

, has been rebuilt several times after fires and earthquakes. It's known for its Italian Renaissance-style facade, and a short distance from the church stands Laoag's symbol, the "Sinking Bell Tower."
The Sinking Bell Tower is a brick tower believed to have been built after the

earthquake. Because the heavy tower was built on soft, sandy ground, it's said to sink about an inch (2.5cm) into the earth every year. Locals say a doorway once tall enough for a person on horseback to ride straight through has grown so low that visitors now have to duck to pass — which has made it a must-photograph landmark for travelers.

The city itself is compact, and you can cover its center in a day; its appeal lies less in sightseeing and more in good food and easy transport. It suits food-loving travelers who enjoy Ilocano cuisine, families touring the northern coast by rental car or chartered van, and anyone doing a loop trip linking Vigan and Pagudpud.
A massive brick tower, grown over with moss and grass, stands slightly tilted. See for yourself how low the doorway has sunk, and catch a photo of the brick glowing red at sunset.
The seat of the Diocese of Laoag, notable for its two-tiered Renaissance-style facade and decorative columns. Outside of Mass hours, you can quietly look around inside.

blocks.title: Aurora Park and the Tobacco Monopoly Monument

children.text: The red-brick monument in the plaza in front of city hall was built in the late 19th century to commemorate the abolition of the Spanish-era tobacco monopoly. In the evening, it fills with locals out for a stroll.

A museum set in a converted old tobacco warehouse, displaying Ilocano household tools, traditional houses, textiles, and artifacts of the mountain peoples. Stopping by on your first day in Ilocos gives real context for the rest of your trip.

blocks.title: A 4x4 tour of La Paz Sand Dunes

children.text: About
15 minutes
from downtown by tricycle, a signature Ilocos activity: racing across the dunes in a modified jeep and riding a sandboard down the slopes.

Two must-try foods: Laoag longganisa, a small, garlicky sausage, and the orange-colored empanada, made from rice-flour dough stuffed with green papaya, egg, and longganisa, then deep-fried. Have it at an evening stall, dipped in spicy vinegar.

blocks.title: A stroll on the Laoag River bridge

children.text: From the bridge crossing the Laoag River on the north side of town, you can see the wide river and, in the distance, the Cordillera mountain range. It's a great evening walking route.

blocks.title: A southern loop through Paoay and Batac

children.text: A half-day route linking Paoay Church, about 30 minutes south of Laoag, Batac's empanada street, and the Marcos Museum and Mausoleum is an essential part of any Laoag trip.

Dinner at an empanada stall and a local restaurant

Return to Laoag for souvenir shopping, then head to the airport or terminal

With an extra day, we recommend heading north on day 3 along the coast to Cape Bojeador Lighthouse, Kapurpurawan Rock Formation, and the Bangui windmills, spending the night in Pagudpud. If you're pairing this with Vigan, it's more efficient to head south from Laoag and stop at Paoay along the way.
Philippine Airlines and Cebu Pacific fly from Manila to Laoag International Airport (LAO), taking about
1 hour 10 minutes
, with one-way fares running about
depending on the season. The airport is about
7km
southwest of downtown, about
15–20 minutes
away by tricycle or taxi. Flight frequency and routes change often, so check with the airline for current schedules.
Several Laoag-bound buses run daily from Cubao, Sampaloc, and Pasay in Manila, including Partas, Fariñas Trans, GV Florida, and Maria de Leon. It takes about
9–11 hours
and the fare is about
depending on class, and a deluxe overnight bus with wide seats is the comfortable choice. Provincial bus fares rose on
September 28, 2026
, so check the fare again when you book.
From Vigan, a bus or van to Laoag takes about
2 hours
; from Pagudpud, heading south takes about
2 hours–2 hours 30 minutes
Taking NLEX–SCTEX–TPLEX and then the La Union and Ilocos Sur coastal road (MacArthur Highway) north takes about
8–10 hours
. If that feels like too much for one day, we recommend an overnight stop in San Juan, La Union, or Vigan along the way.
The cathedral, bell tower, Aurora Park, and museum downtown are all within walking distance of each other, and short tricycle trips in town run about
A half-day loop to Paoay and Batac typically runs about
for a chartered tricycle, while a full-day tour up to the northern coast usually runs about
for a van with driver.
Traditional horse-drawn carriages called calesas also run in town. They are cheap at about
per person for a city ride (as of
April 2026

), and the city hall is preparing to improve the calesa routes and offer experience packages linking the market and restaurants. Taking a calesa once between the cathedral and Aurora Park is also a very Laoag experience.
Ilocos Norte has one of the most clearly defined dry seasons in the Philippines.
November–May
brings almost no rain, which is great for walking downtown and touring the dunes, and
December–February
is the most pleasant, with cool mornings and evenings. In
March–May
, midday temperatures climb to around
, so plan to rest in a museum or cafe during the hottest hours.
June–October
is the rainy season, affected by the southwest monsoon and typhoons, and flight and bus cancellations or delays are common, especially in
July–September
, when typhoons frequently cross northern Luzon. On the festival side, the Pamulinawen Festival is held around the city's founding anniversary (
February 10
) in
February
, filling the city with street parades and performances.

Accommodations cluster around downtown near the cathedral and Aurora Park, making it easy to walk to restaurants and sights. A clean mid-range hotel runs about
a night, and a budget pension around
. If you want a resort with a pool and spacious grounds, Fort Ilocandia, a large, long-established resort by the coastal dunes south of downtown, is a popular choice with families.

Laoag is the true home of Ilocano food. Be sure to try Laoag longganisa, a small, plump, strongly garlicky sausage; bagnet, twice-fried pork; pinakbet, a vegetable stew flavored with bagoong (fermented fish sauce); poqui-poqui, sautéed grilled eggplant and egg; and dinengdeng, a vegetable soup. La Preciosa, a long-running downtown restaurant, has long been known for its Ilocano home cooking and thick carrot cake. For souvenirs, Ilocos vinegar, chicharon corn snacks, and basi, a sugarcane wine, all make good choices.
The best time for bell tower photos is
4–6 PM
, when the brick glows red. The tower sits right by the road, so be careful crossing.
Sharing a sand dune 4x4 with several other people cuts the per-person cost significantly — try finding companions in your accommodation's lobby.
Before setting off on a chartered tricycle, agree clearly on the stops, waiting time, and total fare.
With relatively few flights, peak-season tickets sell out early. If you're taking the bus, book your return ticket in advance too.
Downtown malls and banks have plenty of ATMs, but cash withdrawals are difficult along the northern coast, including Pagudpud, so withdraw enough in Laoag before heading out.
Museum and church hours can change on Mondays or public holidays, so check before you visit.
If you're doing a loop trip linking Vigan to the south and Pagudpud to the north, plan on about two nights in Laoag as a comfortable midway base.
You can check event schedules such as the Pamulinawen Festival and attraction operating notices on the
Ilocos Norte provincial official website
During typhoon season in
July–September
, flights to Laoag Airport can be cancelled en masse. In this period, build in a buffer to get back to Manila the day before your international flight home.
The Sinking Bell Tower is an old structure — don't go inside it or climb its walls.
The sand dune 4x4 ride goes down steep slopes at speed. Skip it if you have back or neck problems or are pregnant, and always wear your seatbelt.
The midday sun in
March–May
is very strong, with a real risk of heatstroke. Bring a hat and water.
On overnight long-distance buses, keep valuables on your person, and don't leave your bags behind when you get off at a rest stop.
Dress modestly inside the church, and refrain from taking photos during Mass.
